claims.normalized_claim: On November 24, 1971 (Thanksgiving Eve), a man who had bought a ticket under the alias 'Dan Cooper' hijacked Northwest Orient Airlines Flight 305, a Boeing 727 flying from Portland, Oregon, to Seattle, Washington; the famous name 'D.B. Cooper' came from a wire-service press error.
counterevidence: The exact mechanism of the 'D.B.' error is disputed; state as 'a wire-service mix-up' without picking one.
allowed_wording: He bought his ticket as 'Dan Cooper'.
The name 'D.B. Cooper' came from a press mix-up.
prohibited_wording: His real name was D.B. Cooper.
The case was on a different flight.
claims.notes: Alias 'Dan Cooper'; 'D.B.' is a press artifact.

claims.normalized_claim: After takeoff he handed a note to a flight attendant indicating he had a bomb, and opened a briefcase showing what appeared to be wires and red sticks.
evidence_locations: FBI ('a note indicating he had a bomb')
allowed_wording: He passed a note claiming he had a bomb.
He opened a briefcase that looked like a bomb.
prohibited_wording: The bomb was real and confirmed.
claims.notes: Bomb claim, not a confirmed device.

claims.normalized_claim: He demanded $200,000 in twenty-dollar bills and four parachutes.
counterevidence: The four were two main and two reserve; one reserve supplied was reportedly an inert training dummy (grade B).
allowed_wording: He demanded two hundred thousand dollars and four parachutes.
claims.notes: Count = four (no source disagreement on the number).

claims.normalized_claim: He was strikingly calm and polite during the hijacking — he lit a cigarette and ordered a bourbon and soda.
evidence_locations: HISTORY (lit a cigarette, ordered a bourbon and soda)
counterevidence: The 'paid his tab / tipped' anecdote is weaker (grade C) — avoid or hedge.
allowed_wording: He stayed calm, lit a cigarette, ordered a bourbon and soda.
claims.notes: Calm demeanor B; omit the C-grade tipping detail.

claims.normalized_claim: The plane landed at Seattle-Tacoma airport, where he released the passengers (commonly reported as about 36) in exchange for the money and parachutes, kept several crew members aboard including the pilot and a flight attendant, and had the aircraft refueled.
evidence_locations: FBI (released passengers, kept crew incl. pilot)
counterevidence: The FBI text gives no passenger number; '36' is secondary — say 'about 36'.
allowed_wording: He let the passengers go in exchange for the money and chutes.
About thirty-six passengers were released.

claims.normalized_claim: He demanded to be flown toward Mexico City at low altitude and low speed, with the aircraft configured so its aft airstair could be used, forcing a planned refuelling stop at Reno.
evidence_locations: FBI ('a course be set for Mexico City')
allowed_wording: He ordered the crew to fly toward Mexico City, low and slow.
prohibited_wording: He demanded to fly to Cuba.

claims.normalized_claim: After the plane took off again, he lowered the Boeing 727's aft airstair and, a little after 8 p.m., parachuted into the night somewhere over a remote, wooded area of southwestern Washington, and was never seen again.
evidence_locations: FBI ('a little after 8 p.m.... jumped out the back... disappearing forever')
counterevidence: Exact jump time (8:11/8:13) and exact location vary; use 'a little after 8 p.m.' and 'somewhere over southwestern Washington'.
allowed_wording: A little after 8 p.m., he jumped from the back of the plane and vanished.
He parachuted into the dark over southwestern Washington.
prohibited_wording: He landed safely at a known spot.
claims.notes: The vanishing — the heart of the mystery. Keep time/location broad.

claims.normalized_claim: He jumped in cold, rainy, near-freezing conditions at night.
counterevidence: Avoid the dramatized '100 mph winds' figure (likely slipstream).
allowed_wording: He jumped into a freezing, rainy night.
claims.notes: Conditions B; raise stakes of the jump.

claims.normalized_claim: The FBI ran a 45-year investigation it codenamed NORJAK, considering more than 800 suspects in the first five years, and calls it the only unsolved hijacking case in the history of U.S. commercial aviation.
allowed_wording: The FBI called it NORJAK and chased it for 45 years.
It is the only unsolved hijacking in U.S. commercial-aviation history.
claims.notes: Scale of the manhunt; the 'only unsolved' line is the hook.

claims.normalized_claim: In July 2016 the FBI suspended its active investigation — suspended, not solved — saying that to solve a case it must prove culpability beyond a reasonable doubt and that none of the tips or new technology had yielded the necessary proof; the man's identity remains unconfirmed.
allowed_wording: In 2016 the FBI suspended the case — suspended, not solved.
The FBI said it never got proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
prohibited_wording: The FBI closed the case as solved.
claims.notes: Suspended != solved. The ending hinges here.

claims.normalized_claim: In 1980, a boy about eight years old, Brian Ingram, found roughly $5,800 of the ransom — decaying twenty-dollar bills in rubber-banded bundles — along the Columbia River at Tena Bar; the serial numbers matched the ransom money, and it is the only ransom cash ever recovered.
evidence_locations: FBI (matched serial numbers, only cash recovered)
counterevidence: Ingram's age is mostly given as 8 (some say 9); spelling Tena/Tina both used; find year 1980 is solid.
allowed_wording: In 1980 a boy found about $5,800 of the money by the Columbia River.
The serial numbers matched; it's the only cash ever found.
prohibited_wording: The find led to an arrest.
claims.notes: The single hard clue — and how little it resolved.

claims.normalized_claim: Among the few physical traces, the hijacker left behind a clip-on necktie on the plane, which investigators later used for microscopic-particle and partial-DNA analysis — none of which has produced a confirmed identification.
counterevidence: Analyses are real but inconclusive — they identified no one.
allowed_wording: He left a clip-on tie behind; decades later it was tested, with no clear answer.
claims.notes: Tantalizing evidence that still resolves nothing.

claims.normalized_claim: Over five decades many people have been named or proposed as suspects — by relatives, authors, journalists, and amateur teams — but the FBI never charged, identified, or confirmed any of them, so no one can be said to be D.B. Cooper, and any living person must never be portrayed as guilty.
allowed_wording: Many names have been proposed over the years; the FBI never confirmed any of them.
No one has ever been proven to be D.B. Cooper.
claims.notes: R2 PROTECTIVE META-CLAIM. Attribute every theory; never assert guilt; confirm any name's living/deceased status before use.

claims.normalized_claim: The FBI's only description of the hijacker is a generic one — a calm, middle-aged man in a dark business suit, white shirt, and thin tie with dark sunglasses — with no photograph and no confirmed identity.
allowed_wording: All anyone has is a description: a calm man in a dark suit and sunglasses.
claims.notes: Visuals must be symbolic only — no real-person likeness, no 'face'.

claims.normalized_claim: The case left a permanent mark on aviation: the FAA required a device later nicknamed the 'Cooper vane' on aircraft with aft airstairs, mechanically preventing the rear stairway from being lowered in flight, and Cooper himself became an enduring American folk-legend.
allowed_wording: The 'Cooper vane' was named after him — it locks the rear stairs in flight.
He became an American legend.
prohibited_wording: He single-handedly created all airport security.

findings: R2 wording locks: UNSOLVED; FBI never confirmed any suspect; never assert anyone 'was D.B. Cooper'; never accuse a living person; suspects were proposed by third parties, not the FBI.
Keep jump time ('a little after 8 p.m.') and location ('southwestern Washington') broad; passenger count 'about 36'; 'Dan Cooper' alias vs 'D.B.' press error.
Durable source content hashes PENDING (FBI bot-protected); non-blocking, capture before publish.
Before broadcast: confirm living/deceased status of any named suspect; lock verbatim FBI quotes on the live pages.
